title: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools
abstract_summary: Language models (LMs) often struggle with basic functionality like arithmetic or factual lookup, despite their impressive zero-shot capabilities. This paper introduces Toolformer, a model trained to autonomously decide which external tools to call, when to call them, and how to use the results for future token prediction. The training process is self-supervised, requiring only a handful of human-written demonstrations for each API. Toolformer incorporates tools such as a calculator, a Q&A system, a search engine, a translation system, and a calendar. Experiments demonstrate that Toolformer achieves substantially improved zero-shot performance across various downstream tasks. Crucially, it achieves this without sacrificing its core language modeling abilities.
problem_and_motivation: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive zero-shot and few-shot performance, yet they suffer from inherent limitations: inability to access up-to-date information, tendency to hallucinate facts, poor performance on low-resource languages, lack of mathematical precision, and unawareness of the progression of time. While scaling models can partially address these, it is inefficient. Existing approaches to integrate external tools either rely on massive human annotations or are restricted to task-specific settings, preventing widespread adoption. The authors propose a novel, self-supervised method to teach LMs to use tools, aiming to overcome these limitations without losing model generality or requiring extensive human labor.
contributions: Introduction of Toolformer, a model that learns to use external tools in a self-supervised manner.
A novel approach to generate training data for tool use by leveraging the in-context learning capabilities of LMs to sample potential API calls.
A filtering mechanism based on perplexity reduction to identify useful API calls without human supervision.
Demonstration that Toolformer achieves competitive or superior zero-shot performance compared to much larger models (e.g., GPT-3) on various benchmarks.
Evidence that tool use can be learned without degrading the model's core language modeling capabilities.

method.overview: The approach equips a language model M with the ability to use tools via API calls. An API call is represented as a tuple (ac, ic) where ac is the name and ic is the input. The model is trained on a dataset augmented with these calls. The process involves three main steps: 1) Sampling potential API calls using in-context learning, 2) Executing these calls to get results, and 3) Filtering calls based on whether they reduce the model's cross-entropy loss for future tokens. Finally, the model is finetuned on the augmented dataset.

components.name: Sampling API Calls
components.description: For each API, a prompt P(x) is used to encourage the LM to annotate text with API calls. The model computes the probability of starting an API call at each position i. Positions with probability above a threshold are selected, and up to m API calls are sampled for each.

components.name: Executing API Calls
components.description: The sampled API calls are executed to obtain a response ri. The response must be a single text sequence.

components.name: Filtering API Calls
components.description: A weighted cross-entropy loss is calculated for the model with and without the API call. A call is kept only if it reduces the loss by at least a threshold τf compared to not using the tool or using it without a response.
components.equations_or_algorithms: Li(z) = - Σ_{j=i}^n w_{j-i} * log pM(xj | z, x1:j-1); L-i - L+i >= τf

components.name: Model Finetuning
components.description: The filtered API calls are interleaved with the original text to create an augmented dataset C*. The model is then finetuned on this dataset using a standard language modeling objective.

method.settings: Language model: GPT-J (6.7B parameters). Dataset: Subset of CCNet. Finetuning: Batch size 128, learning rate 1e-5, linear warmup for 10% of training. Training infrastructure: 8 NVIDIA A100 40GB GPUs using DeepSpeed ZeRO-3.

tasks_and_datasets.name: LAMA (SQuAD, Google-RE, T-REx)
tasks_and_datasets.metric: Accuracy (lenient: correct word in top 5 predictions).

tasks_and_datasets.name: Question Answering (WebQS, NQ, TriviaQA)
tasks_and_datasets.metric: Percentage of generations containing the correct answer in the first 20 words.

tasks_and_datasets.name: Multilingual QA (MLQA)
tasks_and_datasets.metric: Percentage of generations containing the correct answer (capped at 10 words).

experiments.setup_details: Zero-shot setup for all tasks. Standard greedy decoding with a modification: the model generates the <API> token if it is one of the top k=10 most likely tokens.

results.takeaway: Toolformer significantly outperforms all baselines, including much larger models.
Toolformer makes effective use of the calculator, more than doubling performance compared to baselines.

ablations_and_analysis.finding: Increasing k increases the frequency of API calls. For k=1, the model is calibrated to use APIs for difficult examples, but this calibration is lost at higher k.
ablations_and_analysis.numbers: T-REx: 40.3% API usage at k=1 vs 98.1% at k=10.

ablations_and_analysis.finding: Tool use ability emerges around 775M parameters.
ablations_and_analysis.numbers: Small models achieve similar performance with or without tools.

limitations: Inability to use tools in a chain (output of one tool as input for another).
No interactive tool use (e.g., browsing search results or refining queries).
Sensitivity to exact input wording when deciding to call an API.
Sample-inefficiency; requires processing millions of documents to generate a few thousand useful calls.
Does not account for the computational cost of making an API call.
failure_modes: Generating API calls that do not provide useful information.
Failing to use tools when they would be beneficial due to prompt sensitivity.
Inability to handle complex, multi-step reasoning tasks requiring chained API calls.
future_work: Developing interactive tool use capabilities (e.g., browsing, query refinement).
Improving sample efficiency through iterative bootstrapping.
Incorporating computational cost into the decision-making process for API calls.

key_claims.claim: LMs can teach themselves to use external tools in a self-supervised way.
Toolformer achieves competitive zero-shot performance with much larger models without sacrificing core language modeling abilities.
The filtering mechanism based on perplexity reduction effectively identifies useful API calls without human supervision.

definitions_and_terms.meaning: A language model finetuned to autonomously decide when and how to use external tools via API calls.
Learning to use tools by generating and filtering API calls based on their impact on language modeling loss, without human-labeled examples for tool use.
A benchmark for evaluating language models as knowledge bases using cloze-style queries.

related_work_positioning: The paper positions Toolformer against existing tool-use approaches that either rely on large-scale human supervision (e.g., Komeili et al., 2022; Thoppilan et al., 2022) or are restricted to task-specific settings (e.g., Gao et al., 2022; Parisi et al., 2022). It highlights that Toolformer is self-supervised and general-purpose. It notes that TALM (Parisi et al., 2022) is the most closely related work, but emphasizes that TALM only explores tool use in settings where the model is finetuned for specific downstream tasks, whereas Toolformer is more general.

sections_summary.summary: Identifies limitations of LMs (hallucinations, lack of up-to-date info, poor math) and proposes Toolformer as a self-supervised solution for tool use.
Describes the three-step process: sampling potential API calls, executing them, and filtering based on perplexity reduction, followed by finetuning.
Details the five tools used: Question Answering (Atlas), Calculator, Wikipedia Search (BM25), Machine Translation (NLLB), and Calendar.
Evaluates Toolformer on various benchmarks (LAMA, Math, QA, Multilingual, Temporal) showing significant zero-shot performance gains.
Investigates the effect of decoding strategy (k) and model size on tool use, finding that tool use ability emerges at scale.
Positions Toolformer against existing literature on tool-augmented LMs and self-training/bootstrapping techniques.
Acknowledges limitations like lack of chained/interactive tool use and summarizes the main contributions.

reproducibility: The paper provides detailed descriptions of the approach, prompts used, and hyperparameters. It uses publicly available models (GPT-J, Atlas, NLLB) and datasets (CCNet, LAMA, MLQA, etc.). The code and data are implied to be reproducible based on the detailed methodology provided.
